attempts.label: DANDI:000248
attempts.entry_title: Illusory contour responses in mouse visual cortex, Neuropixels (Shin et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: The Neuropixels findings mostly held, but the two-photon and holography findings could not be tested. IC-encoders were found in all six visual areas, and decoding of illusory-contour inference worked in V1 and most other areas. The exclusively center-responsive V1 neurons did not reproduce (44 units against 18), nor did their responses to illusory and real edges or their orientation match, possibly because the selection procedure differs. Stronger higher-area input to IC-encoders appeared in every analysis variant, but a tie of medians in one left it undecided. The findings on the causal role of IC-encoders in pattern completion could not be tested, as the imaging and holography recordings are not in the dataset.
attempts.description: Tests the Neuropixels findings of Shin, Ogando, Abdeladim and colleagues (2025) on dandiset 000248, which holds 12 Neuropixels sessions with six probes in V1, LM, RL, AL, PM and AM while mice viewed illusory contour images. It counts the units and the IC-encoders and segment responders, selects exclusively center-responsive V1 units, repeats the analyses on fixed-gaze trials, computes cross-correlograms between V1 and higher visual areas, and decodes the images and the inference of the illusory contour from each area. The 2p imaging and holography data of the paper are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Limiting the Neuropixels analysis to fixed-gaze trials (pupil within 8 degrees of its modal position) leaves 11 exclusively center-responsive V1 RS units, and their responses to ICs and orientation match do not change the conclusion.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 2b to 2e legends; Results, Mouse V1 neurons respond to ICs despite the absence of contrast within their receptive fields, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: When analyzing only fixed-gaze trials, there were n = 11 exclusively center-responsive V1 RS units; 10 sessions had eye tracking data and of these, 9 sessions had a valid receptive field mapping block where the fixed-gaze constraint left at least one trial in each position
outcomes.notes: Ten sessions have eye tracking, as in the paper. Under rule (r), any fixed-gaze RF trial counts for the coverage of the 9 positions, 9 sessions are valid, the paper's number; under rule (s), standard trials only, 8 are (session 630506 has no fixed-gaze standard trial at one position). Under rule (r) and fig1e reading (a), 10 exclusively center-responsive V1 RS units remain (within 11 +/- 1.1, in two sessions), and the orientation match (71.4% to 100% across tests and blocks, 7 to 9 IRE-responsive units) is above the shuffle 95th percentile (50.0% to 77.8%) in every combination. Under fig1e reading (b), 41 units remain. The units under rule (s) are the same 10, so the unit count rests on the session rule only through the session count. The fixed-gaze selection rests on the fig1e selection, which gives 44 units with all trials against the paper's 18, so the match of the fixed-gaze count may be partly coincidental.
deviations: The 8 degree threshold of the Methods cannot be applied, as the files give pupil position in camera pixels with no conversion; the code's 20 pixels (criterion reading b) is used.

Assumption. The criterion and the Extended Data Fig. 2 legend require that fixed-gaze RF trials cover all 9 positions ("at least one trial in each position") without saying whether inverse trials count. Rule (r), any RF trial, is adopted, as neither text restricts the trials to standard patches; it gives the paper's 9 sessions, where standard trials only give 8. A valid session with no fixed-gaze standard trial at a position gets p = 1 there. Asked of the authors under findings (methods_unavailable).
The shuffle 95th percentile of 1,000 permutations is the criterion's standard choice for the null of the match.

outcomes.notes: The groups hold 79 V1 IC-encoders and 526 V1 segment responders, the paper's numbers. In all 8 combinations of smoothing (boxcar, Gaussian), flank (raw, corrected) and measure (fraction, number of connected HVA units), IC-encoders have the larger mean and P(IC-encoder > segment responder) from 0.62 to 0.64, with a tie-corrected two-sided rank-sum p from 1.0e-05 to 3.9e-04 (paper 7.0e-06). outcomes.statement: A linear SVM decodes the four images IC1, LC1, LC2 and IC2 from V1 activity in the Neuropixels data with tenfold cross-validation accuracy above the chance of 0.25.
outcomes.source: Figure 3a; Results, Representation of IC inference across the mouse visual cortical hierarchy, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: The tenfold cross-validation performance was substantially above chance, indicating that neural activity patterns evoked by these four images were highly distinct at the multivariate level
outcomes.notes: V1 accuracy 0.697 +/- 0.052 under reading (a) and 0.719 +/- 0.056 under reading (b), against the chance of 0.25, signed-rank p = 0.00049 under both, 12 of 12 sessions above 0.25 (range 0.268 to 0.887 under reading a). The other areas range from 0.48 (AM) to 0.709 (LM) under reading (a).

outcomes.statement: In Neuropixels V1, TRE trials are decoded as the matching IC image more often than as the matching LC image (0.51 against 0.22), so IC inference is represented in V1.
outcomes.source: Figure 3c; Results, Representation of IC inference across the mouse visual cortical hierarchy, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Applying inference decoding to Neuropixels V1 recordings revealed that T RE was substantially more likely to be decoded as I C than as L C (Fig. 3c ; decoding probability for I C vs. L C was 0.51 vs. 0.22, P < 0.05 Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b), P(TRE -> IC) = 0.518 and P(TRE -> LC) = 0.210, both within tolerance, IC above LC in 10 of 12 sessions, signed-rank p = 0.0024. Under reading (a), 0.516 and 0.197, the LC value 0.0014 below the lower bound 0.198, same p. With two further cross-validation seeds, both values are within tolerance under both readings, reading (a) IC 0.513 and 0.511, LC 0.198 and 0.199, p = 0.0024 (decoding_checks_shin_2025.ipynb), reading (b) IC 0.519 and 0.514, LC 0.209 and 0.215, p = 0.0015 and 0.0068 (decoding_seed1_shin_2025.ipynb, decoding_seed2_shin_2025.ipynb), so the outcome does not depend on the seed.
deviations: The decoder is scikit-learn's libsvm SVM, not MATLAB's fitcecoc; reading (b) searches C from 10^-3 to 1 with one-vs-one coding in place of the code's Bayesian search. On the first outer fold of the V1 sessions, C above 1 gave a lower best inner accuracy in all 12 (by 0.005 to 0.064), from fits that partly did not converge (12 to 17 of 36 per C value), and the one-vs-all coding changed the best inner accuracy by -0.012 to 0.024 (decoding_checks_shin_2025.ipynb).

outcomes.statement: In the Neuropixels data almost every visual area decodes TRE as IC more than as LC, significantly in V1, LM, RL, AL and PM and not in AM, with V1, LM and AL the strongest.
outcomes.source: Figure 3d legend; Results, Representation of IC inference across the mouse visual cortical hierarchy, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: In the Neuropixels dataset, almost every visual area was substantially biased toward decoding T RE as I C than L C , with V1, LM and AL showing the strongest representations of the IC
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b), adopted, the first seed gives four areas that decode TRE as IC significantly more than as LC (V1 p = 0.0024, LM 0.0156, RL 0.0049, AL 0.0020; PM 0.077, AM 0.083), with LM, V1 and AL the three largest mean scores (0.346, 0.308, 0.285). The two further seeds give five significant areas each, V1, LM, RL, AL and PM (PM p = 0.0425, AM p = 0.083) and V1, LM, RL, AL and AM (AM p = 0.0186, PM p = 0.052), with LM, V1 and AL the three largest. Under reading (a), five areas are significant with all three seeds (V1, LM, RL, AL and AM; PM p = 0.092 with the first seed) and V1, LM and AL are the three largest. The criterion is met in five of six runs. V1, LM, RL and AL are significant and LM, V1 and AL the three largest in all six; only the fifth area changes, and PM p runs from 0.0425 to 0.092 and AM p from 0.0020 to 0.083. The statement names PM as significant and AM as not; that set appears only with reading (b) and seed +100000, and the criterion counts areas without naming them. Sessions per area 12, 8, 11, 10, 12, 11, as in the paper.
deviations: Assumption. The Methods do not say how the SVM hyperparameters were set; the paper's code chooses them with OptimizeHyperparameters. Reading (b), C chosen by an inner cross-validation, is adopted as the reading closer to the code. It searches C from 10^-3 to 1 with one-vs-one coding. On the first outer fold of each session of V1, PM and AM, C above 1 gave a higher best inner accuracy in 1 of 35 sessions (PM, by 0.001), from fits that mostly did not converge (PM 28 to 30 and AM 30 of 33 or 36 per C value), and the one-vs-all coding changed the best inner accuracy by -0.026 to 0.027, which could change the chosen coding in some sessions; its effect on the inference scores was not computed (decoding_checks_shin_2025.ipynb). Asked of the authors under findings (methods_unavailable).

Assumption. The cross-validation partition is random, and reading (b) meets the criterion with two of three seeds (the first seed gives four significant areas). The outcome follows the majority of the seeds, a rule chosen after the first seed's result and not stated in the criterion. A rule requiring every seed would give partially reproduced; averaging the per-session scores over the seeds was not computed.
The decoder is scikit-learn's libsvm SVM, not MATLAB's fitcecoc.

44 exclusively center-responsive units under reading a and 52 under reading b, against 18 +/- 1.8. The V1 RS count of 1,804 matches. It asked for a count of fig1e units before the exclusivity step, to locate where 44 or 52 diverge from 18.

10 sessions have eye tracking. Only 8 sessions are valid, against the paper's 9, and the criterion requires an exact match. A session counts as valid only if its fixed-gaze standard RF trials cover all 9 positions, while the legend says "at least one trial in each position"; session 630506 covers 8 positions with standard trials only, and counting inverse trials was not tried (problem 4).

Friedman p = 0.356 for reading a and 0.898 for reading b, both >= 0.05. For trials whose eye frames are all NaN, the area_max variant becomes -inf, so its range prints as NaN or inf (problem 9).

outcomes.notes: The paper's code skips sessions 5, 14 and 43 of AllenSDK's session table for movie one presentations marked invalid (extract_natural_movie_neuropixels.m lines 19 and 101 at ac3300b). In ascending session id over the 58 sessions of dandisets 000021 and 000022 these are sub-718643564, sub-719828686 and sub-769319621, the three sessions of the 58 whose files hold an invalid_times interval tagged stimulus that overlaps natural movie one (239 and 954 frames of natural_movie_one_presentations in the two Brain Observatory 1.1 sessions; sub-703279277 and sub-716813540 have such intervals that miss the movie). Of the 26 Functional Connectivity sessions, sub-769319621 is the only such one: 1497 frames of its 60-repeat movie block fall in the interval, its longest repeat lasts 30.719 s (30.042 s at most elsewhere) and its longest gap between frames is 0.133 s (0.050 s at most elsewhere). No session has an incomplete repeat. Dropping it and the 2 sessions without V1 units leaves 23 sessions, as the paper says, each with 75 bins. With the good units the 1725 pooled slopes have median 1.116, outside 0.9 to 1.1 (reading 1) and inside 0.85 to 1.15 (reading 2); the criterion counts either reading. With the Methods' criteria alone, median 1.129, the same under both readings. Keeping sub-769319621 (24 sessions) gives medians 1.119 and 1.131.
deviations: The 60-repeat block of natural movie one is the table natural_movie_one_more_repeats_presentations in these files. Bins run from the onset of their first frame to the end of their twelfth (0.37 to 0.50 s).

The excluded session is identified by AllenSDK's rule for invalid presentations (a presentation overlapping an invalid_times interval tagged stimulus, ecephys_session.py lines 645 to 680), which the paper's code relies on, and by putting the 58 session ids in ascending order, the order of AllenSDK's session table, to read the code's indices; here a frame counts when its onset lies in the interval. This is an assumption, since the Methods say only that 3 sessions were excluded "due to truncation of movies or absence of V1 units", and no repeat in dandiset 000022 is incomplete. The count of 23 sessions is reached only with this reading of the paper's code.
Units labelled good as well as passing the Methods' criteria (the assumption of data-v1-units); the Methods' criteria alone give the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: Linear SVM decoding accuracy of image identity decreases monotonically as the slope increases, above the chance level of 1/119.
outcomes.source: Figure 2B; Results, Neural variability structure enables maximal discriminability, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: As expected, cross-validation accuracy decreases monotonically as a function of log-mean vs. log-variance slope.
outcomes.notes: Run in part, at as-is and slopes 0 and 1 over the 30 sessions and at slope 2 over the first four included sessions (good units, claim's seed). The 150 decodings at as-is, slopes 0 and 1 and the shuffled data took 17.8 minutes on 4 CPUs (medians 28 s as-is, 16 s at slope 0 and 27 s at slope 1 per 10-fold decoding of the original data; at most 115 s original and 138 s shuffled). At slope 2 the four decodings took 342 to 496 s (median 398 s, 8.3 minutes in parallel), so slope 2 over the 30 sessions is estimated at 50 minutes on 4 CPUs and the criterion's 22 conditions at about 5.4 hours (time between slopes 1 and 2 interpolated linearly, a rough estimate), over the sixty-minute notebook limit (protocol, Develop on a subset). In the part that ran, accuracy is higher at slope 0 than at slope 1 in 30 of 30 sessions (means 0.787 against 0.424, Wilcoxon p = 1.9e-09) and higher at slope 0 than as-is (0.403, p = 1.9e-09); in the four sessions run at slope 2 it is below as-is in each (0.212, 0.188, 0.132 and 0.134 against 0.356, 0.255, 0.185 and 0.446). Every session is above the chance level 1/119 = 0.0084 at every condition run (lowest 0.132). The criterion needs slope 2 in every session and every 0.1 step, so the claim is not judged. Slope 2 alone over 30 sessions, which would allow the criterion's partial judgement, fits a notebook of its own by this estimate but was not run in this revision: with it the entry's run would have passed the time left.

outcomes.statement: Destroying pairwise noise correlations by shuffling trials within stimulus for each neuron changes how decoding accuracy and RSM similarity depend on the slope.
outcomes.source: Figure S4C; Discussion, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: When we destroyed the pairwise noise correlation structure by shuffling the trial order for each neuron within each trial type, both the decoder accuracy and the representation similarity analysis showed an altered dependence on the log-mean vs. log-variance slope (Figure S4C).

statistics.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank test across sessions or session pairs, original against shuffled

outcomes.notes: Each neuron's trials shuffled within stimulus before the slope change. Decoding (2B), at the conditions run, with the same trial order and folds for original and shuffled data: 0.435 shuffled against 0.403 original as-is (Wilcoxon p = 5e-05) and 0.764 against 0.787 at slope 0 (p = 0.029). Within-session RSM similarity (4C): different at 16 of 21 slopes and as-is (as-is p = 3.9e-07); the shuffled curve peaks at 1.0, the original at 1.1. Across-session RSM similarity (4E): different at all 21 slopes and as-is (p = 1.4e-29 as-is); the shuffled curve peaks at 1.3, the original at 1.1. All three analyses differ at one or more slopes. The claims file makes this claim depend on fig2b-decoding-falls-with-slope, blocked for the cost of its 22 conditions; this comparison needs only the decoding at the conditions run, so it is tested. The comparisons were run under the claim's seed only, so how much the seed matters is not known.
deviations: Decoding compared at as-is and slope 0 only, for the cost given under fig2b-decoding-falls-with-slope. The shuffle uses the claim's second generator for the RSMs and its first for the decoding, not the code's np.random.seed(0) sequence. Since round 2 the decoding of the shuffled data uses the seed of fig2b-decoding-falls-with-slope for the trial order and folds, as the original does, and the claim's seed only for the shuffle.

findings.statement: The ICwcfg1 presentations table lists every 400 ms frame of the block, including the gray inter-trial frames, under one column frame. The gray frames show the same image as the Blank stimulus (template 0), and nothing marks which of them are Blank trials. The image codes 0 to 21 have no names in the files or the dandiset metadata; the names come only from the paper's code. The trials can be recovered from the sequence (60 leading gray frames, then trial and gray frame alternating, 400 Blank trials in every session), and the templates agree in kind with the code's names.
The units table describes none of its columns (quality, isi_violations, firing_rate and the others read "no description").

The spikes share the clock of the ICwcfg1 table. The V1 population rate rises 75 ms after image onsets and not after Blank onsets, and the image identity is decoded from the 400 ms after onset (0.576, chance 0.083) and not from the 400 ms before (0.089). No session is deposited twice. All 11 sessions the paper's code lists are present, with a twelfth (sub-619293) that it does not list.

paper_notes.statement: The Methods select units by isi_violations, amplitude_cutoff and presence_ratio. The unit counts (64 +- 25, 1920 in all) and the across-neuron slope (1.048) match only when units not labelled good are also dropped, as AllenSDK does by default (filter_by_validity). Question for the authors, were the units those of AllenSDK's default units table? This attempt assumed so for every claim on the Allen data.

The paper excludes 3 of 26 Functional Connectivity sessions for truncated movies or no V1 units, without naming them. In dandiset 000022 no session has an incomplete repeat of natural movie one and 2 have no V1 quality units. The paper's code names the third: it skips sessions whose movie one presentations AllenSDK marks invalid (extract_natural_movie_neuropixels.m lines 19 and 101), which is sub-769319621, whose movie block overlaps an invalid_times interval tagged stimulus and has repeats up to 30.72 s long. The Methods' word truncated does not describe this.

entries.title: Trial-to-trial variability geometry in mouse V1 (Kim and Shin 2025)
entries.description: Tests Kim and Shin (2025) on dandiset 000248, the Allen OpenScope Illusion data the paper uses for its Isomap pictures, and, as data elsewhere, on the Allen Visual Coding Neuropixels sessions of its main analyses, as deposited in dandisets 000021 and 000022. It changes the slope of the log-mean against log-variance relation of V1 spike counts by rescaling residuals and measures manifold overlap, continuity, dimensionality, geodesic geometry, alignment and representational consistency.

entries.description: Tests the Neuropixels findings of Shin, Ogando, Abdeladim and colleagues (2025) on dandiset 000248, which holds 12 Neuropixels sessions with six probes in V1, LM, RL, AL, PM and AM while mice viewed illusory contour images. It counts the units and the IC-encoders and segment responders, selects exclusively center-responsive V1 units, repeats the analyses on fixed-gaze trials, computes cross-correlograms between V1 and higher visual areas, and decodes the images and the inference of the illusory contour from each area. The 2p imaging and holography data of the paper are not in the dandiset.
